Introduction

This article follows [4] and [5], referred to as I and II. The numbering of its sections continues that of II (which contains §§ 1 through 4). To refer to a result of II, we simply give its number. For example: (3.2.17).

In I, we set out the yoga underlying II and the present article III. Nevertheless, II and III are logically independent of I. They do not contain all the results announced in I.

In II, we set out the Hodge theory of nonsingular algebraic varieties (not necessarily complete). Here we treat the case of arbitrary singularities. Beginning with § 7, essential use will be made of the results of §§ 1 through 3 of II.

In the case of a complete singular algebraic variety X, the fundamental idea is to use resolution of singularities to “replace” X by a simplicial system of smooth projective schemes X_•.

⟦P0002-A01 — simplicial diagram⟧

(or, as we shall say, by a smooth projective simplicial scheme). The results of §§ 5 and 6 make it possible to find such simplicial schemes X_• having, in a suitable sense, the same cohomology as X. One may then “express,” by means of a spectral sequence, the cohomology of X in terms of that of the X_n. In accordance with the general principles of I, one may then use classical Hodge theory on each X_n and thereby deduce a mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of X.

In the case of an arbitrary algebraic variety X, one “replaces” X by a smooth simplicial scheme X_•, compactified by a smooth projective simplicial scheme X̄_•. One further arranges that X̄_n − X_n is a normal-crossings divisor, a union of smooth divisors D_{n,i}. One then “expresses,” by means of a spectral sequence, the cohomology of X in terms of the cohomology of the p-fold intersections of the D_{n,i} (n ≥ 0, p ≥ 0), and deduces a mixed Hodge structure on H^•(X).

Sections 5 and 6 constitute a summary (without proofs) of the theory of “cohomological descent.” This theory, in the more general framework of topoi, is set out by B. Saint-Donat in S.G.A.4, V bis.

In § 7, no. 1, certain previously obtained results are recast in the language of filtered derived categories. No. 2 contains a proof of the two-filtrations lemma simpler than the one in § 1, no. 3.

The forbidding no. 1 of § 8 is the heart of this work. The essential result is Theorem (8.1.15). In its proof, in order to apply the two-

In no. 2, the mixed Hodge structure on H^n(X, ℤ) is defined (X a separated scheme). It is shown that the Hodge numbers h^{pq} of H^n(X, ℤ) can be nonzero only for (p, q) ∈ [0, n] × [0, n]. For n > dim X, there is a more precise result (8.2.4). If X is smooth (respectively, complete), they can be nonzero only if, in addition, p + q ≥ n (respectively, p + q ≤ n). If X is a complete closed subscheme with complement U in a complete smooth scheme Z of dimension n, then, following N. Katz, one may interpret this “duality” between the complete and smooth cases as arising from “Alexander duality”

… H^i(Z, ℚ) → H^i(X, ℚ) → (H^{2n−i−1}(U, ℚ))^* → H^{i+1}(Z, ℚ) …

From the functoriality properties of the theory constructed, one deduces the useful Corollaries (8.2.5) through (8.2.8), which are stated in terms independent of any Hodge theory.

In § 8, no. 3, the cohomology of every simplicial scheme X_• is endowed with a mixed Hodge structure. This generality is not illusory.

a) Relative cohomology spaces can be interpreted as the cohomology of suitable simplicial schemes.

b) Let B_G be the classifying space of the Lie group underlying an algebraic group G. The cohomology of B_G can be interpreted as that of a suitable simplicial scheme.

In § 9, no. 1, after computing the mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of B_G (for G linear), one deduces that of G. As a corollary, one finds that if a linear group G acts on a complete nonsingular variety X, then the map

H^•(X, ℚ) → H^•(X, ℚ) ⊗ H^•(G, ℚ)

factors through H^•(X, ℚ) ⊗ H^0(G, ℚ) ⊂ H^•(X, ℚ) ⊗ H^•(G, ℚ).

In § 10, mixed Hodge structures purely of type {(−1, −1), (−1, 0), (0, −1), (0, 0)} (III.0.5) are interpreted in terms of abelian schemes, and H^1 of curves is considered in detail.

The theory developed thus far is an absolute theory (the functors Rf_* are not studied), and concerns only constant coefficients. I conjecture that if 𝓗 is a polarizable variation of Hodge structures (in the sense of Griffiths [6]) on a scheme X, then the cohomology of X with coefficients in the local system 𝓗 carries a natural mixed Hodge structure. I can prove this only when X is complete.

5.1. Simplicial topological spaces.

This subsection begins with reminders for which one may refer to the Strasbourg homotopy seminar, 63/64.

Hom(𝒜, ℬ) = the category of functors from 𝒜 to ℬ.

δ_i : Δ_n → Δ_{n+1} = the increasing injection such that i ∉ δ_i(Δ_n) (0 ≤ i ≤ n + 1).
s_i : Δ_{n+1} → Δ_n = the increasing surjection such that s_i(i) = s_i(i + 1) (0 ≤ i ≤ n).
ε : Δ_{−1} → Δ_n = the unique map from Δ_{−1} to Δ_n.
(Δ^+) = the category whose objects are the Δ_n (n ≥ −1), and whose arrows are the increasing maps between the Δ_n.
(Δ) = the full subcategory of (Δ^+) whose objects are the Δ_n (n ≥ 0).
(Δ^+)_k = the full subcategory of (Δ^+) whose objects are the Δ_n (k ≥ n).
(Δ)_k = the full subcategory of (Δ^+) whose objects are the Δ_n (k ≥ n ≥ 0).

For k ≥ −1, the skeleton functor sq_k is the restriction functor

sq_k : Hom((Δ)^o, 𝒞) → Hom((Δ)_k^o, 𝒞).

The coskeleton functor cosq_k is the right adjoint to sq_k

5.2. Cohomology of simplicial topological spaces.

(5.2.1) To every simplicial topological space X_• there is attached an ordinary topological space |X_•|, called its geometric realization (see below). In the special case where the X_n are discrete, one recovers the usual notion of the geometric realization of a simplicial set.

In [14], G. Segal defines the cohomology of X_• with values in an abelian group A to be H^•(|X_•|,A). Under suitable hypotheses, the filtration of |X_•| by its successive skeleta gives a spectral sequence.

(5.2.1.1) E_1^{pq} = H^q(X_p,A) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X_•,A).

One advantage of this definition is that it applies equally well, for example, to the definition of groups K(X_•). We shall adopt another definition, better suited to sheaf-theoretic techniques.

Geometric realization. — For an integer n ≥ 0, let |Δ_n| denote the simplex in ℝ^{Δ_n} whose vertices are the set of basis vectors. We identify Δ_n with the set of vertices of |Δ_n|. Every function f : Δ_n → Δ_m extends linearly to |f| : |Δ_n| → |Δ_m|.

(x_m, |f|(a)) ≡ (f(x_m), a)   (mod R).

The geometric realization of X_• is, by definition,

|X_•| = Y/R.

Definition (5.3.4). — A continuous map a : X → S is of cohomological descent if the augmentation morphism of cosq(X → S),

((X/S)^{Δ_n})_{n≥0} → S,

is of cohomological descent. We say that a is of universal cohomological descent if, for every u : S′ → S, the continuous map a′ : X ×_S S′ → S′ is of cohomological descent.

(5.3.5) The fundamental results, proved in S.G.A.4, V bis, are as follows.

(I) Continuous maps of universal cohomological descent form a Grothendieck topology on the category of topological spaces.

It is called the topology of universal cohomological descent.

9.1. Cohomology of groups and classifying spaces.

Let G be a connected complex linear algebraic group. We propose to calculate the mixed Hodge structure on H^•(G). We shall first calculate that on H^•(B_{•G}), by reduction to the case of tori; we shall then calculate that on H^•(G) via the Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequence (6.1.5). As a bonus, we obtain the curious Theorem (9.1.7).

Theorem (9.1.1). — Let G be a linear algebraic group. One has H^{2n+1}(B_{•G},ℚ)=0, and H^{2n}(B_{•G},ℚ)⊗ℂ is purely of type (n,n) (III.0.5).

Let G^0 be the identity component of G and let T⊂G^0 be a maximal torus. Since

H^•(B_{•G},ℚ)=H^•(B_{•G^0},ℚ)^{G/G^0},

by the splitting principle (see (6.1.6)) one has

H^•(B_{•G},ℚ) ↪ H^•(B_{•T},ℚ).

This inclusion is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures: it suffices to treat the case of a torus, indeed, by the Künneth formula, the case G=G_m. Here are two proofs of (9.1.1) in this case.

First proof. — The cohomology of G_m (=the projective line minus two points) is H^0=ℤ, H^1=ℤ. The only Hodge numbers h^{pq} of H^1(G_m) that could be nonzero are h^{01}=h^{10} and h^{11} ((8.2.4)(i)(iv)). Since h^{01}+h^{10}+h^{11}=2h^{01}+h^{11}=1, one has h^{01}=0 and H^1(G_m) is purely of type (1,1) (for another proof, see (10.3.8)). The term E₂^{p,q} of the spectral sequence (6.1.5), zero for p+q odd, is therefore purely of type ((p+q)/2,(p+q)/2). Its abutment has the same homogeneity.

Second proof. — One knows that ℙ^r(ℂ), equipped with 𝒪(1), is an “approximation” to B_{G_m}: the homomorphism [𝒪(1)]:H^i(B_{•G_m})→H^i(ℙ^r(ℂ)) is bijective for i≤2r. The cohomology group H^{2i}(ℙ^r(ℂ)) is generated by the cohomology class of an algebraic cycle (namely, a linear subspace), and is therefore of type (i,i). The following proposition allows one to deduce that H^{2i}(B_{G_m}) is of type (i,i).

10.2. 1-motives and biextensions

The results of this subsection will not be used in the sequel of this section. We shall use the notion of biextension (S.G.A. 7, VII (2.1)) and the following generalization.

(10.2.1) Let K_i:[A_i→B_i] (i=1,2) be two complexes of sheaves, concentrated in degree 0 and −1 (on an arbitrary topos). A biextension of K_1 and K_2 by an abelian sheaf H consists of:

a) a biextension P of B_1 and B_2 by H, i.e. an H-torsor P over B_1×B_2, with P_{b_1,b_2} depending biadditively on b_1 and b_2;
b) a trivialization (= biadditive section) of the biextension of B_1 and A_2 by H obtained by inverse image from P;
c) a trivialization of the biextension of A_1 and B_2 by H obtained by inverse image from P; the trivializations b) and c) are required to coincide over A_1×A_2.

The category of biextensions of K_1 and K_2 by H is denoted Biext(K_1,K_2;H). It is a Picard category (its objects may be added). The group Biext^0(K_1,K_2;H) of automorphisms of any biextension of K_1 and K_2 by H is

Biext^0(K_1,K_2;H)=Hom(H^0(K_1)⊗H^0(K_2),H).

The group of isomorphism classes of biextensions is denoted Biext^1(K_1,K_2;H). As in (S.G.A. 7, VII (3.6.5)), one verifies that

Biext^i(K_1,K_2;H)=Ext^i(K_1⊗^L K_2;H)     (i=0,1).

From this formula, or elementarily, one verifies that if K_i′→K_i is a quasi-isomorphism (i=1,2), giving a biextension of K_1 and K_2 by H is equivalent to giving a biextension of K_1′ and K_2′ by H.

This still applies when “sheaves” is replaced by “algebraic groups” (respectively “complex analytic groups”): these may be interpreted as sheaves on a suitable site.

M:[X→G].

Over ℂ, one likewise has Biext^0(M_1^{an},M_2^{an};G_m)=0.

Indeed, every biadditive morphism G_1×G_2→G_m is trivial.

10.4. Translation of a theorem of Picard.

(10.4.1) Let 𝓗 be a mixed Hodge structure such that h^{pq}=0 for p or q<0 (respectively for p or q>n). I shall provisionally denote by I(𝓗) (respectively II_n(𝓗)) the 1-motive defined by the largest mixed Hodge substructure of (𝓗_ℤ/torsion)(1) (respectively by the largest quotient of (𝓗_ℤ/torsion)(n)) that is purely of type

{(−1,−1),(−1,0),(0,−1),(0,0)}.

If X is a complex algebraic variety of dimension ≤N, I conjecture that the 1-motives I(H^n(X,ℤ)), II_n(H^n(X,ℤ)) (for n≤N), and II_N(H^n(X,ℤ)) (for n≥N) admit a purely algebraic definition. The morphisms

T_ℓ(I(H^n(X,ℤ)))→(H^n(X,ℤ_ℓ)/torsion)(1)
T_ℓ(II_n(H^n(X,ℤ)))←H^n(X,ℤ_ℓ)(n)     (for n≤N)
T_ℓ(II_N(H^n(X,ℤ)))←H^n(X,ℤ_ℓ)(N)     (for n≥N)

and their analogues in de Rham cohomology should likewise admit a purely algebraic definition. This is what we have verified when dim(X)=1. Here is another example.

(10.4.2) Let S be a smooth projective surface, U a dense (Zariski) open subset of S, and C=S−U. Put

H_2^{log}(U,ℤ)=Ker(H_2(U,ℤ)→H_2(S,ℤ)).

According to [8] § 9, this group does not depend on the chosen smooth compactification S of U. Modulo finite groups, it is simply (3.2.17) W_{−3}H_2(U,ℤ) (H_2(U,ℚ), dual to H^2(U,ℚ), is equipped with the dual mixed Hodge structure). One can verify that the 1-motive defined by (H_2^{log}(U,ℤ)/torsion)(−1) has the following description:

a) By Poincaré duality, H_2(U,ℤ)=H_c^2(U,ℤ). The long exact cohomology sequence of (S,C) gives an exact sequence

H^1(S,ℤ)→H^1(C,ℤ)→H_2^{log}(U,ℤ)→0.

b) Let H_m^1(C) be the quotient of Pic^0(C) by its unipotent radical. It is known that H^1(C,ℤ)=T_ℤ(H_m^1(C)) and H^1(S,ℤ)=T_ℤ(Pic^0(S)). There is therefore a map

H_2^{log}(U,ℤ)→T_ℤ(H_m^1(C)/Pic^0(S)),

which is an isomorphism modulo finite groups.

c) The map deduced from b)

(10.4.2.1)     (H_2^{log}(U,ℤ)/torsion)(−1)→T_ℤ(H_m^1(C)/Pic^0(S))

is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures (and an isomorphism modulo finite groups).

(10.4.3) We shall not prove the preceding constructions and compatibilities. The result is implicit in the following theorem of E. Picard ([11], volume I, p. 62). Here P and A denote polynomials.

Every residue of the double integral

∬ P(x,y)dxdy/A(x,y)

may be regarded as a logarithmic or cyclic period of an Abelian integral.

I recall that:

a) A k-fold integral on a nonsingular projective variety V of dimension d is a closed rational k-form on V: it is an element α∈H^0(U,Ω^k), for U a dense open subset of V, satisfying dα=0. Here k=2 and V=ℙ^2, so that k=dim V and the condition dα=0 is vacuous.

b) A k-fold integral α defines an element, again denoted α, of H^k(U,ℂ). The periods of α are the numbers ⟨α,c⟩ for c∈H_k(U,ℤ). If c is defined by a singular chain C, then

⟨α,c⟩=∫_C α.

c) The residues of a k-fold integral α∈H^0(U,Ω^k) are the numbers ⟨α,c⟩ for

c∈Ker(H_k(U,ℤ)→H_k(V,ℤ)).

In the case considered by Picard, the map H_2(U,ℤ)→H_2(ℙ^2,ℤ) is zero, and there is no need to distinguish between periods and residues. For the general case, cf. Lefschetz, [10], note I.

d) By “logarithmic or cyclic period of an Abelian integral,” Picard means simply “period of a simple integral β on a curve Y.” It is understood that β and Y are determined rationally by P and A.
